name: Aritar
tagline: Lampokhari Lake, an 1895 dak bungalow and a gentle Silk Route start
meta_description: Aritar in East Sikkim: Lampokhari Lake boating, the 1895 dak bungalow, Mankhim hilltop, homestay costs, how to reach and why no permit is needed.
summary: Aritar is a farming village at about 1,400–1,500 m in Pakyong district, East Sikkim, and the gentlest first stop on the Silk Route. It has Lampokhari Lake with rowing boats, a dak bungalow built in 1895 by John Claude White, a Kagyu gompa and the hilltop Rai temple at Mankhim. No Protected Area Permit is needed.
intro: Aritar lies about 67 km from Gangtok, 52 km from Kalimpong and 30 km from Rangpo, on the slopes above the Rangpo River valley in Pakyong district. Terraced fields and cardamom groves step down the hill between scattered houses, and the centre of village life is Lampokhari, a long, narrow lake at around 1,400 m with forest on its banks and a walking path around it. It is one of very few lakes in Sikkim where you can take a rowing boat out. Most travellers spend one night here on the way up to Zuluk.

Aritar was a stop on the old trade line from Kalimpong through Pedong and Rhenock to Rongli, Zuluk and Jelep La, and it became a small administrative post under the British-era Sikkim government. John Claude White, the first Political Officer in Sikkim, had a dak bungalow built here in 1895, and Sikkim's first police outpost and treasury were set up on the same premises in 1897. The bungalow, known locally as Ari Bangla, still stands on the ridge above the lake.

Aritar is below the Silk Route permit point, so Indian travellers need no permit here, and foreign nationals with the standard Sikkim Restricted Area Permit can visit too. That makes it a good base for mixed groups who cannot all go on to Zuluk. Stays are registered village homestays and small lodges around the lake and up towards Mankhim, most charging ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals, indicative 2026. Evenings are quiet; bring a torch, a book and an appetite for dal-bhat and gundruk.

story.title: John Claude White's bungalow above the lake
paras: In 1889 the British posted John Claude White to Gangtok as the first Political Officer of Sikkim, a job he held until 1908. In the years after the Chogyal Thutob Namgyal was sidelined, White ran much of the state's day-to-day administration, reorganising land revenue, forests and roads. Aritar, on the trade path to Tibet and close to the Darjeeling district border at Rhenock and Pedong, was a useful place for a post. In 1895 he had a dak bungalow built here, a rest house where officials could break a journey.

Two years later, in 1897, Sikkim's first police outpost and its first treasury were set up on the same premises. That is why the bungalow turns up in local histories as a small piece of how modern Sikkim came to be governed. White wrote about these years in his 1909 book, Sikhim and Bhutan: Twenty-one Years on the North-East Frontier. Today the building, known locally as Ari Bangla, still stands on its ridge, and the walk up to it gives a fine view over the lake.

Aritar's people are older than the bungalow. Local histories, summarised on Wikipedia, say Lepcha families were the first settlers in the Rhenock area and Bhutia families from Tibet founded villages here, Aritar among them, from the mid-16th century. Nepali-speaking Gorkha families came later, many from the late 19th century. Today the village is a mix of all three, the gompa above the lake follows the Kagyu tradition, and Nepali is what you will hear in the tea shops.
story.source: Wikipedia: Aritar, Sikkim; John Claude White; Rhenock. J. C. White, Sikhim and Bhutan (1909)

did_you_know: Sikkim's first police outpost and first treasury were opened in 1897 on the premises of the Aritar dak bungalow, built two years earlier.
Mankhim, on the hilltop above Lampokhari, has a temple of the Rai community, a Kirati people, at about 6,500 ft.
John Claude White, who built the Aritar dak bungalow, is also credited with introducing apple growing to Lachung and Lachen in North Sikkim.
facts: None for Indians; RAP for foreigners

highlights.title: Rowing on Lampokhari Lake
highlights.text: Lampokhari is a narrow lake at about 1,400 m with forest along its banks, a walking path around the edge and rowing boats for hire. Go early, before day-trippers arrive, when the water is still and the reflections of the trees are sharp.

highlights.title: Ari Bangla, the 1895 dak bungalow
highlights.text: John Claude White, the first British Political Officer in Sikkim, had this rest house built in 1895, and Sikkim's first police outpost and treasury opened on its premises in 1897. The short walk up from the lake gives a wide view over the valley.

highlights.title: Mankhim hilltop and Rai temple
highlights.text: Above the lake, Mankhim rises to about 6,500 ft, with a temple of the Rai community and views across the hills to the Kangchenjunga range on clear mornings. You can walk up through forest from the lake or drive most of the way and walk the last part.

highlights.title: Aritar gompa
highlights.text: The village monastery above the lake follows the Kagyu tradition and is known for its traditional architecture and painted murals. Visit in the morning, walk clockwise round the building, and leave a small donation if you go inside. It is a calm hour away from the lakeside crowds.

highlights.title: A Silk Route taster with no permit
highlights.text: Because Aritar is below the Rongli permit point, it works for everyone: families with young children, seniors who should not go higher, and foreign travellers who cannot enter Zuluk. You get village life, a lake and the history of the trade route without the altitude or the paperwork.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from Siliguri and Gangtok to Rhenock and Rongli, mostly leaving in the morning; from either town a local taxi up to Aritar takes 20–40 minutes. Expect roughly ₹250–400 a seat from Siliguri and ₹150–250 from Gangtok, plus ₹500–900 for the last stretch, indicative 2026. Ask at the stand the day before.

A small car from NJP or Bagdogra costs about ₹5,000–7,000 and takes 4–5 hours, via Rangpo and Rorathang, or via Kalimpong and Pedong when NH10 is cut. From Gangtok, about 67 km, budget ₹3,500–5,000 one way. Most Silk Route packages stop here on night one. Check current status before you travel.

The nearest railhead is New Jalpaiguri (NJP) and the nearest working airport is Bagdogra (IXB), both near Siliguri, about 4–5 hours away. Pakyong Airport is closer, about 40 km, but has no scheduled flights as of 2026. The Sivok–Rangpo railway is still being built. Check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Aritar has no big hotels. Most beds are in registered village homestays and small family lodges, some around Lampokhari Lake, some along the road towards the dak bungalow, and a few higher up at Mankhim with wider views. Rooms are plain and clean, usually with attached bathrooms and geyser or bucket hot water, and meals are home-cooked. Expect ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with dinner and breakfast, indicative 2026. We do not name individual houses because standards change; ask your driver or agent which homestays are registered and open, and pick Mankhim if you want sunrise views.
budget_tip: Take a shared jeep to Rhenock and a local taxi up to Aritar instead of a reserved car from NJP; for two people it can save ₹3,500 or more.
tips: Walk the lake path early in the morning, before day-trippers from Gangtok and Rangpo arrive.
The walk up to Mankhim is steep, roughly 600 m of climb in about 3 km; seniors should go most of the way by car.
Carry cash from Rangpo, Rhenock or Gangtok, as card payments and ATMs are unreliable in the village.
If you are heading to Zuluk next morning, make sure your driver has the Protected Area Permit papers ready before you leave Aritar.
Leeches are common on forest paths from June to September, so wear closed shoes and carry a little salt.

experiences.title: Rowing on Lampokhari Lake at first light
experiences.cost: ₹50–200 per person for a boat, indicative
experiences.summary: Lampokhari is a long, narrow lake at about 1,400 m in the middle of Aritar, with forest on its banks, a walking path and boats for hire. An early row or a slow walk around the edge is the simplest pleasure of a night in Aritar.
body: Lampokhari sits in a fold of the hill below Aritar bazaar. The name is usually read as Nepali for a long pond, and that is what it looks like from above: a slim sheet of water, around 1,400 m up, with trees on both sides and a path running round. It is one of very few lakes in Sikkim where you can take a boat out, which is why weekend day-trippers from Rangpo, Pakyong and Gangtok come in good numbers.

Go early. In the first hour after sunrise the water is still and the reflections are clean, and you may have the place almost to yourself. Boats are hired at the small jetty when it opens in the morning; rates are low, roughly ₹50–200 per person, indicative 2026. Children must wear the life jackets provided. If you prefer to stay ashore, the walk around the lake takes 30–45 minutes at an easy pace.

After the lake, walk or drive up to Ari Bangla, the 1895 dak bungalow on the ridge, for the view back down over the water. In spring the slopes around the lake carry flowering trees, and in October and November the air is clear and dry. During the monsoon months the paths are slippery and leechy, and boating may stop after heavy rain. Ask your homestay about the opening time on the day.

faqs.q: Is boating allowed on Lampokhari Lake in Aritar
faqs.a: Yes. Lampokhari is one of very few lakes in Sikkim where you can hire a boat. Boats run from a small jetty, usually from morning to late afternoon, at roughly ₹50–200 per person, indicative 2026. Life jackets are provided and children must wear them. Boating may pause after heavy rain or during local events, so ask your homestay in the morning.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk around Lampokhari Lake
faqs.a: About 30–45 minutes at an easy pace on the path around the lake. The path is mostly level, with a few uneven and muddy patches, so wear proper shoes rather than sandals. Seniors can manage it comfortably with breaks. In the monsoon months from June to September, watch for leeches and slippery stones near the water.

faqs.q: Is Lampokhari Lake crowded
faqs.a: It can be on weekends and holidays, when day-trippers come from Rangpo, Pakyong and Gangtok, mostly between late morning and mid-afternoon. Early mornings and weekdays are quiet. If you are staying overnight in Aritar, walk down at sunrise and again in the late afternoon, when the light is softer and the crowds have gone.

experiences.title: Walk to Ari Bangla, the 1895 dak bungalow
experiences.summary: A short walk from Lampokhari Lake up to the dak bungalow John Claude White built in 1895, where Sikkim's first police outpost and treasury opened in 1897. Small building, big story, and a wide view over the lake and valley.
body: John Claude White arrived in Sikkim in 1889 as the first British Political Officer, and for the next two decades he ran much of the state's administration. Dak bungalows were part of that work: plain rest houses along the main routes where officials, surveyors and travellers could sleep and change ponies. Aritar, on the trade path from Kalimpong to Jelep La, got one in 1895. Locals still call it Ari Bangla, the Aritar bungalow.

In 1897 Sikkim's first police outpost and its first treasury were set up on the same premises. It is worth a moment to imagine that: a small ridge-top building, a few constables and a strongbox, at a time when most of Sikkim had no police at all. White described these years in his 1909 book, Sikhim and Bhutan: Twenty-one Years on the North-East Frontier, which you can find in libraries and online archives.

The walk up from the lake takes 15–25 minutes on a road and path. Whether you can go inside depends on the caretaker and on official bookings, so treat the interior as a bonus. The building and the view from its lawn over Lampokhari are the reason to go. Combine it with the gompa nearby for a slow morning, and carry water, as there are few shops on the ridge.

faqs.q: Who built the Aritar dak bungalow and when
faqs.a: The Aritar dak bungalow, known locally as Ari Bangla, was built in 1895 under John Claude White, who served as the first British Political Officer of Sikkim from 1889 to 1908. Two years later, in 1897, Sikkim's first police outpost and treasury were set up on the same premises. These facts are recorded in the Wikipedia articles on Aritar and on White.

faqs.q: Can tourists go inside the Aritar dak bungalow
faqs.a: Sometimes. The bungalow is a government building, and access to the interior depends on the caretaker and on whether it is in official use. Many visitors only see it from outside, which is still worthwhile for the building and the view over Lampokhari Lake. Ask your homestay or at the gate politely, and do not enter closed rooms without permission.

faqs.q: How far is the dak bungalow from Lampokhari Lake
faqs.a: It sits on the ridge above the lake, a 15–25 minute walk up by road and path, or a few minutes by car. The climb is moderate, so most people manage it easily with a break or two. Go in the morning or late afternoon for softer light on the lake below, and combine it with a visit to Aritar gompa nearby.

experiences.title: Hike to Mankhim and the Rai hilltop temple
experiences.cost: Free on foot; ₹800–1,500 by local taxi, indicative
experiences.summary: Mankhim is the hilltop above Lampokhari, at about 6,500 ft, with a temple of the Rai community and views to the Kangchenjunga range on clear mornings. Walk up through forest from the lake, or drive most of the way and walk the last part.
body: From Lampokhari Lake, Mankhim is about 3 km away and roughly 600 m higher, at about 6,500 ft. The forest trail climbs steadily through mixed trees and village fields, with a few steep pitches. Fit walkers take 1–1.5 hours up; allow less for the way down but more care, as the path can be slippery. If anyone in your group should not climb, a local taxi can take you most of the way by road.

At the top is a temple of the Rai, a Kirati people whose traditional faith centres on ancestors and nature. Treat it as a working place of worship: remove shoes where asked, do not climb on structures, and ask before photographing people at prayer. On clear mornings, especially in October and November, you can see the Kangchenjunga range to the north-west, with the forested ridges of East Sikkim all around you.

A few registered homestays sit on the Mankhim ridge for those who want to sleep high and watch the sunrise from there. Carry water and a snack, as there are few shops on the way. In the monsoon, from June to September, the trail is muddy and full of leeches and the views are usually hidden in cloud, so in those months we would drive up by local taxi or skip Mankhim altogether.

faqs.q: How difficult is the walk from Aritar to Mankhim
faqs.a: It is a moderate hike: about 3 km each way with around 600 m of climb, taking 1–1.5 hours up for most fit walkers. The path has some steep and uneven stretches and gets slippery after rain. Wear proper walking shoes and carry water. Seniors and young children can go most of the way by car instead and walk only the last short section.

faqs.q: What is the Mankhim temple
faqs.a: Mankhim has a temple of the Rai community, a Kirati people of the eastern Himalaya, set on the hilltop above Aritar at about 6,500 ft. It is an active place of worship for the local Rai community rather than a tourist sight. Visit quietly, follow any instructions about shoes and photography, and leave a small donation if you wish.

faqs.q: Can you see Kangchenjunga from Mankhim
faqs.a: Yes, on clear days. From the Mankhim ridge the Kangchenjunga range shows to the north-west, best in the early morning from October to December and in the dry spells of March to May. Cloud usually hides it from June to September. If the view matters, sleep at a Mankhim homestay and look out at dawn, when the sky is most often clear.

experiences.title: A quiet hour at Aritar gompa
experiences.summary: Aritar's village monastery follows the Kagyu tradition and is known for its traditional architecture and painted murals. A morning visit, a slow walk round the building and a few minutes inside the prayer hall is a calm counterweight to the busy lakeside.
body: Aritar gompa sits on the slope above Lampokhari and serves the Buddhist families of the village and the hamlets around it. It belongs to the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, one of the main traditions in Sikkim, and the building is in the familiar Sikkimese style: a sloping roof, painted woodwork, prayer wheels along the walls and murals inside showing the Buddha, great teachers of the lineage and protector deities, painted in strong colours.

Mornings are best. If monks or village elders are at prayer, sit quietly at the side and wait until they finish before you move about. Walk clockwise round the building and turn the prayer wheels with your right hand. Remove shoes before entering the prayer hall, keep hats off and voices low, and ask before taking photographs inside, as some monasteries do not allow it. Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered.

There is no ticket. A small donation in the box near the entrance, ₹20–100, is customary and goes to the upkeep of the gompa. Combine the visit with Ari Bangla, the old dak bungalow on the same ridge, and a walk down to the lake for a full slow morning. During Losar, the Tibetan new year in February or March, the village is busier and the monastery may hold special prayers.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Aritar monastery
faqs.a: No. Aritar gompa is free to visit. A small donation of around ₹20–100 in the box near the entrance is customary and helps with upkeep, but it is not required. Remove your shoes before entering the prayer hall, walk clockwise round the building, keep voices low and ask before taking photographs inside, as rules can differ from one monastery to another.

faqs.q: Which tradition does Aritar gompa follow
faqs.a: Aritar gompa belongs to the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, one of the main monastic traditions in Sikkim alongside the Nyingma. It serves the Buddhist families of Aritar and nearby hamlets, many of them of Bhutia descent. The building is known for its traditional architecture and painted murals, which are worth a slow look in good morning light.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to visit Aritar gompa
faqs.a: Morning is best, when the light is good on the murals and the gompa is quiet. If prayers are under way, sit at the side and wait. Afternoons are also fine, but you are more likely to find the prayer hall locked if the caretaker is away. Combine the visit with the dak bungalow and the lake for an easy half-day.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Aritar
faqs.a: Indian nationals do not need any special permit for Aritar, because it lies below the Silk Route permit point at Rongli. Foreign nationals need only the standard Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, which is free and issued online or at entry points such as Rangpo. A Protected Area Permit is needed only if you go on to Zuluk and beyond. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Aritar from Gangtok and NJP
faqs.a: Aritar is about 67 km from Gangtok, roughly 2.5–3 hours by road via Rorathang. From NJP or Bagdogra it is about 110–115 km and 4–5 hours, either via Rangpo and Rorathang or via Kalimpong and Pedong when NH10 is blocked. From Kalimpong it is about 52 km. Roads in the monsoon can be slow, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Aritar
faqs.a: October to May is best. October and November bring clear skies and mountain views from Mankhim; December and January are cold but bright; March to May are mild and green with flowering trees. We avoid June to September, when rain, leeches and landslides on the approach roads make travel slow and views rare. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days should we spend in Aritar
faqs.a: One night works if you are on the way to Zuluk; you get the lake in the evening and early morning. Two nights let you add the walk to Mankhim, the gompa and the dak bungalow without rushing, and suit families who will not go higher. Aritar also makes a calm last night on the way back down from the Silk Route.

faqs.q: Is Aritar good for families with small children
faqs.a: Yes. At about 1,400–1,500 m it carries no real altitude risk, the lake has boats with life jackets, the walk around it is mostly level, and homestays are relaxed about children. It is also below the permit zone, so no paperwork for young children. Keep them close to the water's edge and carry warm layers for evenings from November to February.

faqs.q: Can foreigners stay in Aritar
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign nationals with a valid Sikkim Restricted Area Permit can visit and stay overnight in Aritar, as it is outside the protected zone. They cannot go on to Zuluk, Nathang or Kupup, which are open only to Indian nationals. Mixed groups often base the foreign members in Aritar while others do the Zuluk loop. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a night in Aritar cost
faqs.a: Registered homestays in Aritar usually charge about ₹1,500–2,500 per person per night with dinner and breakfast, indicative 2026. Add ₹50–200 for a boat on the lake, ₹50 Sikkim tourist fee per person at check-in, and transport. A reserved car from NJP costs about ₹5,000–7,000; shared jeeps to Rhenock plus a local taxi cost far less.

faqs.q: Is Lampokhari Lake natural
faqs.a: Lampokhari is usually described as one of the older natural lakes in Sikkim, though its banks and jetty have been built up for visitors, and some travel writers call it artificial. What is certain is that it is one of very few lakes in the state where boating is allowed. It sits at about 1,400 m in the middle of Aritar village.

faqs.q: What food can we eat in Aritar
faqs.a: Food is simple and home-cooked: rice, dal, seasonal vegetables, chicken or egg curry, and Sikkimese extras such as gundruk, the fermented leafy greens, and chhurpi, the local cheese, if you ask. Small shops near the lake sell momos, noodles, tea and snacks at ₹60–150 a plate. Vegetarian meals are easy to arrange with your homestay.
